chapter_title: Control Flow: Branches, Loops, and Sequences
chapter_summary:
Now that you understand how to store and manipulate data with variables, the next crucial step in Blueprint scripting is learning how to control the order in which your logic executes. This is known as **control flow**. Without control flow, your Blueprint would simply run from top to bottom, executing every node regardless of game state or player input. Control flow nodes allow your game to make decisions, repeat actions, and manage complex event chains, bringing your game to life.

The most fundamental control flow node is the **Branch** node, often referred to as an "If-Else" statement. It takes a single Boolean input, typically the result of a comparison or a Boolean variable. If the condition is `true`, the execution flows out of the "True" pin; if `false`, it flows out of the "False" pin. This is incredibly powerful for decision-making. For example, you might use a Branch to check `if (PlayerHealth <= 0)` before executing a "PlayerDied" event, or `if (DoorIsOpen)` before allowing a character to walk through. You can chain multiple Branch nodes together to create more complex conditional logic, but be mindful of readability; too many nested branches can become difficult to follow. A common mistake is forgetting to connect both the "True" and "False" pins if both paths require subsequent actions, or connecting the wrong condition to the Branch. Always double-check your Boolean inputs.

Beyond making decisions, you often need to repeat actions. This is where **loops** come in. Unreal Engine provides several types of loop nodes, each suited for different scenarios. The **For Loop** is used when you need to iterate a fixed number of times. It takes a "First Index" (usually 0) and a "Last Index" as input. For each iteration, it outputs an "Index" (the current loop count) and an "Loop Body" execution pin, which fires once per iteration. Once all iterations are complete, the "Completed" execution pin fires. This is perfect for spawning multiple enemies, generating a grid of objects, or applying damage over time a specific number of times.

When you need to iterate over a collection of items, such as an array of inventory items or a list of enemies, the **For Each Loop** is your best friend. It takes an Array as input and, for each element in that array, it outputs the "Array Element" itself, its "Index" in the array, and fires the "Loop Body" execution pin. Like the For Loop, it has a "Completed" pin. This is incredibly efficient for processing all items in a player's inventory, updating the state of all active projectiles, or checking conditions on every enemy in a level.

The **While Loop** is another type of loop that continues to execute its "Loop Body" as long as a given "Condition" (a Boolean) remains `true`. This loop type requires careful handling because if the condition never becomes `false`, you'll create an **infinite loop**, which will freeze your game or even crash the editor. To prevent this, it's often essential to include a **Delay** node within the While Loop's body, especially when dealing with game logic that runs over multiple frames. The Delay node pauses execution for a specified duration before continuing, allowing the game to render frames and process other events. Without a Delay, a While Loop can consume all CPU resources. A common safe practice is to use "Do N" or "Do Once" nodes in conjunction with While Loops if you need to limit their execution, or to ensure that the loop condition is guaranteed to become false after a certain number of iterations or a specific game state change.

Finally, the **Sequence** node allows you to execute multiple, independent execution paths from a single input. When the Sequence node receives an execution pulse, it fires its "Then 0" pin, then "Then 1," then "Then 2," and so on, in order. This is useful for organizing your Blueprint graph, especially when an event triggers several distinct actions that don't depend on each other's completion. For example, when a player picks up an item, a Sequence node might simultaneously update the UI, play a sound effect, and add the item to the inventory. While it executes paths in order, the paths themselves are independent and don't wait for each other to complete unless explicitly chained.

Mastering these control flow nodes is essential for building dynamic and responsive game logic. Imagine a scenario where a player interacts with a quest giver. A Branch node could check if the player has already completed the quest. If not, a For Each Loop could iterate through the player's inventory to see if they have the required items. If they do, a Sequence node could then simultaneously update the quest status, remove the items, and grant a reward. By combining variables with these control flow structures, you gain the power to create truly interactive and engaging gameplay experiences.

screens.title: Control Flow: Branches, Loops, and Sequences
screens.subtitle: Decide, repeat, and order Blueprint logic to create responsive gameplay

narration.text: Control flow is the backbone of interactive game logic. In Blueprints, control flow decides which nodes run and when they run, letting your game react to player actions, repeat behaviors, or coordinate multiple responses. You will learn the Branch node for conditional decisions, three loop types for repetition, and the Sequence node for organizing multiple independent outcomes. Each structure has practical trade-offs: Branch makes clear yes/no choices, For and For Each loops let you repeat work across counts or arrays, and While loops require care to avoid infinite loops. The Sequence node helps you trigger several actions from a single event without tangled connections. I will show concrete examples you can implement: checking player health with a Branch, spawning actors in a line with a For Loop, iterating inventory with For Each, and using a Delay inside a While Loop to keep the game responsive. By the end you will be able to combine these nodes safely to build quests, spawn systems, and repeated checks. Think about one gameplay action you want to control — a door that opens only if the player has a key — and imagine which node or nodes make that simple and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Why control flow matters
keyIdea.text: Control flow lets you implement decisions, repetition, and ordered actions that make gameplay dynamic and correct. Choosing the right node keeps Blueprints readable and safe.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Control Flow
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Control Flow: Branches, Loops, and Sequences

Learn how to make decisions, repeat actions safely, and run multiple outcomes from a single event using Blueprint control-flow nodes.

In this lesson

You will explore Branch, For Loop, For Each Loop, While Loop with Delay, and Sequence nodes, and see practical patterns to avoid common pitfalls like infinite loops.

Explore Key Topics
Branch
Decide between true/false paths for gameplay conditions.
Loops
Repeat actions by count or across arrays; use Delay with While loops.
Sequence
Trigger multiple independent actions from one event without tangled wiring.
Coming up

A hands-on spawn-and-check Blueprint guides you step by step. Expect practical checks and debugging tips.

Visual Concept
Decision, Repeat, Sequence — the three roles of control flow.
Blueprint Pattern
Pattern
Use Branch for conditions, For/For Each for predictable repetition, While with Delay for timed checks, and Sequence for multi-action triggers.
Quick Tip
Always ensure loop termination. Prefer Delay inside While loops so the engine can update frames.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will gain and why they matter

narration.text: These objectives focus your practice on four essential control-flow skills. First, you will implement conditional logic with the Branch node so your game can choose between two paths based on a Boolean test. Practically, that means checking flags or comparisons like player health or a door state before running further actions. Second, you will use For Loop and For Each Loop nodes to repeat work: For Loop for a fixed iteration count and For Each to walk arrays of items or actors. Knowing when to use each prevents redundant code and keeps performance predictable. Third, you will learn the While Loop pattern and its safe usage. While loops repeat while a condition is true, but without a Delay or a guaranteed exit they cause infinite loops. You will practice adding a Delay or limiting iterations with Do N to keep the game responsive. Fourth, you will manage ordering with the Sequence node to trigger multiple independent actions from one event, simplifying your graphs. Each objective includes a measurable milestone so you can verify competency as you build the hands-on Blueprint.

keyIdea.title: Practiced outcomes
keyIdea.text: By practicing these objectives you will be able to author safe, readable Blueprints that perform decisions, repeated work, and parallel actions reliably.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Milestones
screens.subtitle: Concrete tasks to verify each objective

narration.text: These practice milestones translate objectives into hands-on checks you can run in the editor. For Branch nodes, implement a check that fires a PlayerDied event when health is zero. Run it, toggle the Boolean, and observe the alternate execution path. For loops: create a For Loop that spawns five actors at spaced positions, verify the Index increments each iteration, and collect the returned actors in an array. For Each loops: populate that array and use For Each to query overlapping actors; print or log each actor name to confirm every element processed. While loops require a guarded example: build a loop that continues while a Boolean is true, but place a Delay node inside and a separate event to flip the Boolean to false. Confirm the loop exits and the editor stays responsive. For Sequence: trigger multiple Print String or effect nodes from one event. Each of these tasks demonstrates not just node usage but safe patterns and debugging checks you can repeat as you learn.

screens.title: What is Control Flow?
screens.subtitle: Definition, role in Blueprints, and practical significance

narration.text: Control flow defines the order and conditions under which parts of your Blueprint graph run. Without explicit control flow, nodes would run without decision, causing unintended effects or wasted computation. In Blueprints, control flow nodes act like traffic signals: they direct execution pulses based on Boolean checks, iteration counts, or an ordered list of outgoing paths. This matters because gameplay depends on conditional behavior — you only want a door to open if the player has a key, or an enemy to spawn a fixed number of times. Control flow also affects performance: repeating expensive work unnecessarily can cause frame drops, so choosing the right loop and ensuring termination is essential. A common misconception is that all loops run asynchronously; in Blueprints, most loop bodies run on the same execution thread unless you explicitly defer work, so blocking loops without Delay will freeze the game. Example: to update 100 actors once per second, use a loop with a Delay or schedule repeated checks with a timer rather than using a tight While loop with no pauses. Key takeaway: design control flow so it expresses intent, keeps graphs readable, and prevents endless execution.

keyIdea.title: Control flow = program behavior
keyIdea.text: Control flow determines what runs, when it runs, and how often, making it essential for correct and performant gameplay logic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is Control Flow?
Definition

Control Flow in Blueprints

Control flow nodes decide execution paths, repeat work, and sequence independent actions. They let your game react and repeat in structured ways.

Why it matters
Correct control flow prevents unwanted behavior and performance problems, and keeps Blueprints maintainable.
Common misconception
Loops run concurrently — incorrect. Most Blueprint loops run synchronously on the game thread; without Delay they block and freeze the editor.
Visuals & Example
Analogy
Think of control flow as the script for NPCs: decisions branch behavior, loops repeat patrols, and sequences schedule simultaneous reactions like sound, animation, and UI updates.
Mini Example
// Pseudocode describing a Blueprint decision
if (PlayerHealth <= 0)
{
  Trigger PlayerDied event;
}
else
{
  Continue gameplay;
}
Key Takeaway

Express intent with clear nodes, guard loops with Delay or limits, and prefer readability over clever wiring.

screens.title: Branch Node (If-Else)
screens.subtitle: Using Boolean conditions to choose execution paths

narration.text: The Branch node is the simplest decision maker in Blueprints. It consumes a Boolean condition and routes execution to a True or False output. Use it whenever game logic diverges depending on state: check if a door is open, if a player has a key, or if health has dropped to zero. For clarity, derive the condition from a named Boolean variable or a comparison node; this makes the graph readable. A common mistake is leaving one execution path unconnected when both outcomes require follow-up actions. Another error is wiring the wrong variable or forgetting to update the Boolean after state changes. Example: use a Branch with condition DoorIsOpen; if True, run the OpenDoor animation; if False, play a locked sound. You can chain Branch nodes to express multiple checks, but deep nesting harms readability. Instead, consider combining conditions with logical operators or extracting checks to functions. When you test a Branch, use Print String nodes to confirm which path runs. Your learner task: create a Branch that checks if PlayerHealth ≤ 0 and calls PlayerDied on True, otherwise continues. That simple test verifies your understanding and shows how branches control flow.

keyIdea.title: Branch controls choice
keyIdea.text: A Branch routes execution into two paths based on a Boolean. Keep conditions explicit and both paths wired when both need work.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Branch Node
Branch

If-Else decisions with Booleans

Use Branch whenever execution should follow one of two paths based on a true/false test.

Good practice
Name your Boolean variables clearly and avoid deep nested branches. Prefer combining checks with logical operators or functions for clarity.
Common mistake
Forgetting to wire both True and False pins when both sides require actions leads to silent bugs.
Concrete Example
Check player death
// Pseudocode representing the Branch test
if (PlayerHealth <= 0)
{
  Trigger PlayerDied event;
}
else
{
  Continue gameplay;
}
Key Takeaway

Use Branch for clear yes/no decisions and always verify both outcomes during testing.

screens.title: For Loop — Fixed Iteration
screens.subtitle: Spawn a fixed number of actors and use Index effectively

narration.text: For Loops run a defined number of times between a First Index and a Last Index. They are ideal when you know how many iterations you need, such as spawning five enemies or building a grid. Each iteration outputs an Index value you can use to position or configure the spawned actor. For example, set First Index to zero and Last Index to four to spawn five cubes. Multiply the Index by a spacing value to place each spawn at a distinct X coordinate. Use the Loop Body execution pin to call Spawn Actor from Class and then add the return value to an array for later processing. After the loop finishes, the Completed pin fires so you can continue with further logic, like starting an overlap check. A mistake beginners make is using the Index as if it were a frame counter — Index is purely the iteration number. Another pitfall is not capturing the returned actor references; without storing them you cannot iterate them later with For Each. Practice: spawn five cubes spaced by Index * 200, store them in a SpawnedCubes array, and confirm each actor appears in the world.

keyIdea.title: For Loop use-case
keyIdea.text: For Loops are best for a known number of repeats and when you need the current iteration index for placement or configuration.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › For Loop
Process

Spawn by count and use Index

Set First Index and Last Index, use Index for positioning, store Return Value to an array, and use Completed for continuation.

Practical pattern
First Index: 0. Last Index: 4. Loop Body: Spawn Actor; Add to SpawnedCubes. Completed: Start checks.
Misuse
Treating Index as time or frame count leads to logic errors. Index is iteration ordinal only.
Concrete Spawn Example
Spawn 5 cubes spaced by Index
// Blueprint pseudocode for spawn placement
FirstIndex = 0
LastIndex = 4
ForLoop(FirstIndex, LastIndex)
  // Loop Body
  Location.X = Index * 200.0
  SpawnedActor = Spawn Actor From Class(Cube, MakeTransform(Location))
  Add Unique(SpawnedCubes, SpawnedActor)
// Completed: Continue
Key Takeaway

Use Index to space or configure each spawned instance and store references for later iteration.

screens.title: For Each Loop — Iterating Collections
screens.subtitle: Process every element in an array safely and efficiently

narration.text: For Each Loop is designed to process every element of an Array. It outputs the current Array Element and its Index, and fires Loop Body once per element. Use For Each when you need to perform the same operation over a collection, for example checking each spawned cube for overlaps or applying damage to every enemy. Unlike a For Loop that iterates a numeric range, For Each directly expresses intent: process this collection. A typical pattern is to feed the SpawnedCubes array into a For Each Loop, call Get Overlapping Actors on each element, then test the overlapping array length with a Greater comparison node and a Branch. When True, print the actor name and adjust its collision as needed. Watch out for mutating the same array you're iterating; removing or reordering elements inside the loop can produce unexpected behavior. If you need to modify the container, consider collecting changes to apply after the loop or iterate a copy. Practically, For Each improves readability and reduces index arithmetic, making array processing straightforward. For Each Loop — Iterating Collections means use for each to process arrays element-by-element. avoid mutating the iterated array mid-loop to prevent unexpected results.. In practical terms, process every element in an array safely and efficiently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: For Each intent
keyIdea.text: Use For Each to process arrays element-by-element. Avoid mutating the iterated array mid-loop to prevent unexpected results.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › For Each Loop
Definition

Iterate arrays element by element

Use For Each to apply the same operation to every element in an array, receiving the element and index each time.

Typical use
Process inventory, update actors, or check properties across a list of objects.
Pitfall
Mutating the same array during iteration can skip elements or corrupt order. Collect changes and apply after the loop when needed.
Concrete Example
Check each spawned cube for overlaps
For Each (SpawnedCubes as Array)
  Overlapping = Get Overlapping Actors(Array Element)
  Length = Length(Overlapping)
  If (Length > 0)
    Branch True: Print "Cube Overlapping: " + Array Element Name
    Set Actor Enable Collision(Array Element, No Collision)
// Completed: continue
Key Takeaway

Use For Each to make array processing explicit and readable; avoid modifying the array while iterating.

screens.title: While Loop — Conditional Repetition and Safety
screens.subtitle: Why Delay and termination matter; safe patterns

narration.text: A While Loop continues to execute its Loop Body as long as a Boolean Condition remains true. This makes it suitable for repeated checks that depend on changing state, such as monitoring whether a player is inside a damage zone. However, While Loops are riskier than For or For Each because if the Condition never flips to false the loop becomes infinite, freezing the editor or crashing the game. To use While safely in Blueprints, include a Delay node inside the Loop Body when the repetition should happen over time; this yields frames back to the engine and prevents busy-waiting. Alternatively, combine While with Do N or a maximum iteration count to guarantee termination. Example pattern: start a While Loop when the player engages an ability, inside it Delay for three seconds, then Branch to check overlap and apply damage if needed; if the player dies or leaves the zone, the Condition becomes false and the loop exits. A common misconception is that Delay moves work to another thread — it does not; it simply waits and yields to the engine so that frames and other systems continue. Always test While implementations carefully with exit triggers.

keyIdea.title: While loop safety
keyIdea.text: Always include a Delay or a guaranteed exit when using While loops to avoid infinite loops and frame stalls.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › While Loop
Definition & Risk

Conditional repetition with careful guarding

While repeats while a Boolean stays true. Use Delay or iteration limits to avoid infinite loops.

Safe patterns
Place a Delay in Loop Body or pair While with Do N or an explicit counter to ensure exit.
Warning
A While loop without Delay can become an infinite loop and block the editor or game thread.
Concrete Example
Damage zone check every 3 seconds
// While Loop pattern
While (IsPlayerAlive)
{
  Delay(3.0)
  If (IsPlayerOnDamageZone)
    ApplyDamage(10)
}
Pro Tip

Prefer a Delay inside the loop for repeated timed checks. Use clear exit conditions and test with a debug toggle switch.

screens.title: Sequence Node — Ordered, Independent Actions
screens.subtitle: Trigger multiple outcomes from a single event

narration.text: The Sequence node accepts a single execution input and emits a series of 'Then' pins that fire in order. Each pin starts an independent execution path immediately after the previous one is triggered. This is ideal for organizing a graph where one event must initiate several distinct actions that do not depend on each other completing. For example, when a player picks up an item, use Sequence to update the UI, play a sound, add the item to inventory, and play a pickup animation. Although Sequence fires paths in order, the actions themselves typically run concurrently if they are non-blocking, so the sound does not wait for the animation to finish. Sequence improves readability by keeping related actions grouped rather than duplicated event wires. A common misuse is to assume Sequence imposes timing guarantees; if you need strict ordering with waits, chain nodes explicitly or include Delay nodes. Use Sequence to keep your graphs tidy and to make intent clear to other designers reading your Blueprint. Sequence Node — Ordered, Independent Actions means sequence initiates multiple independent paths from one trigger, improving clarity. do not rely on it for timing guarantees without explicit waits.. In practical terms, trigger multiple outcomes from a single event. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sequence organizes actions
keyIdea.text: Sequence initiates multiple independent paths from one trigger, improving clarity. Do not rely on it for timing guarantees without explicit waits.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Sequence Node
Core Concept

Start multiple actions cleanly

Sequence helps you fire several independent execution paths from a single entry, keeping graphs tidy and intentional.

When to use
Trigger UI updates, sounds, and inventory changes together when an item is picked up or an event occurs.
Misconception
Sequence is not a timing primitive. If you need precise sequencing over time, add Delay or chain actions explicitly.
Example
Item pickup actions
Sequence Then 0: Update UI. Then 1: Play sound. Then 2: Add to inventory. Then 3: Update quest log.
Key Takeaway

Use Sequence to reduce wiring complexity and show related actions clearly from one trigger.

screens.title: Combining Nodes — A Quest Example
screens.subtitle: Branch, For Each, and Sequence working together

narration.text: Combining control-flow nodes allows complex mechanics while keeping each part focused. Consider a quest where the player must hand in several required items. Start with a Branch to check if the quest is already complete; if it is, exit. If not, use a For Each Loop to iterate the player's inventory array and count required items. For each matching element, increment a counter or remove the item from inventory. Once the For Each completes, use a Branch to compare the collected count against the requirement. If satisfied, trigger a Sequence to award the reward, update the quest status, and play completion effects. This pattern separates concerns: Branch decides eligibility, For Each gathers data, and Sequence initiates side effects. A common pitfall is mixing UI updates into the loop body instead of collecting changes and applying them after Completed; that can cause inconsistent UI state. Test each stage with Print String to reveal intermediate values and ensure counters and removals behave as expected. Combining Nodes — A Quest Example means use branch to gate logic, for each to evaluate collections, and sequence to trigger independent side effects for a clean, testable flow.. In practical terms, branch, for each, and sequence working together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Combine nodes for clarity
keyIdea.text: Use Branch to gate logic, For Each to evaluate collections, and Sequence to trigger independent side effects for a clean, testable flow.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Quest Example
Scenario

Hand in required items for a quest

Branch checks completion, For Each scans the inventory, and Sequence issues rewards and updates once the requirement is met.

Why this structure
It keeps the observable effects (UI, sound, inventory changes) separated from data collection, which eases testing and debugging.
Testing tip
Add Print String after the For Each Completed pin to log the collected count before branching to reward logic.
Step Outline
  1. Branch: Is quest already complete? If yes, exit.
  2. For Each: Iterate inventory and count matching items.
  3. Branch: If count meets requirement, Sequence: grant reward, remove items, update quest.
Key Takeaway

Compose nodes to separate data checks from side effects; this yields easier testing and fewer hidden bugs.

screens.title: Hands-on: BP_SpawnerAndChecker — Spawning Logic
screens.subtitle: Implement the For Loop to spawn and store cubes

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through the spawning portion of BP_SpawnerAndChecker. Begin with Event BeginPlay and add a For Loop. Set First Index to zero and Last Index to four to spawn five cubes. Inside the Loop Body, build a Make Transform and a Make Vector node to set the spawn location. Multiply Index by 200.0 for the X component to space cubes along a line. Use Spawn Actor From Class to create the actor and then Add Unique to push the returned actor into a SpawnedCubes array variable. Naming the array clearly helps later processing. After the last iteration the Completed pin fires, ready to start overlap checks. A common debugging step is to add a Print String inside the Loop Body showing the Index and the SpawnedActor name so you can verify each spawn during play. If a cube doesn't appear, check that the mesh is set, collision is enabled, and the spawned location is not inside geometry. This exercise reinforces the relationship between loop index and object placement and how storing references enables subsequent loops to inspect those instances.

keyIdea.title: Spawn and store
keyIdea.text: Use For Loop Index to space spawns and store each returned actor in an array for later processing with For Each.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Spawner — For Loop
Task

Spawn 5 cubes and store them

Use Event BeginPlay → For Loop (0 to 4) → Spawn Actor From Class. Connect Index to Make Vector X multiplied by 200.

Checklist
  • First Index = 0, Last Index = 4
  • Multiply Index by 200 for spacing
  • Add returned actor to SpawnedCubes array with Add Unique
Code Walkthrough
Event BeginPlay
ForLoop(FirstIndex=0, LastIndex=4)
  Location.X = Index * 200.0
  Spawned = Spawn Actor From Class(ActorClass=Cube, Transform=MakeTransform(Location))
  Add Unique(SpawnedCubes, Spawned)
// Completed -> For Each Check
Key Takeaway

Store spawn references immediately so you can iterate them later; use Print String to confirm each spawn during testing.

screens.title: Hands-on: BP_SpawnerAndChecker — Overlap Checking
screens.subtitle: Use For Each and Branch to detect overlaps and react

narration.text: After spawning, the next step is to iterate the SpawnedCubes array with a For Each Loop to check overlapping actors for each cube. Feed SpawnedCubes into For Each; for each Array Element call Get Overlapping Actors, then get the Length of that returned array. Compare Length with zero using a Greater (Integer) node to produce a Boolean. Connect that Boolean to a Branch. On True, call Print String with a prefix like "Cube Overlapping: " plus the array element's name so you see which cube overlaps in the viewport logs. To avoid repeated reports for the same overlap, set the actor's collision disabled after printing by calling Set Actor Enable Collision with No Collision as the new mode. This ensures the same overlap doesn't trigger multiple prints. Be careful that disabling collision changes the actor state; if later logic relies on collision, document this change or restore it when appropriate. Testing tip: artificially place cubes close together in the editor to force overlaps and observe the printed messages. This full pattern demonstrates how For Each, Branch, and actor functions combine to inspect and mutate actor state safely.

keyIdea.title: Check, branch, respond
keyIdea.text: Use For Each to examine each spawned actor, Branch to decide, and actor calls to change state based on outcomes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Checker — For Each + Branch
Task

Iterate spawned cubes and detect overlaps

Use For Each on SpawnedCubes, call Get Overlapping Actors for each element, test Length > 0 with Branch, then react on True.

Reaction pattern
Print overlapping cube name and disable its collision to avoid duplicate messages.
Walkthrough
For Each (SpawnedCubes)
  Overlapping = Get Overlapping Actors(Array Element)
  If (Length(Overlapping) > 0)
    Branch True:
      Print String("Cube Overlapping: " + Array Element Name)
      Set Actor Enable Collision(Array Element, No Collision)
// Completed: done
Debug Tip

Use Print String liberally while testing to confirm element names and branch results, then remove or switch to logging once stable.

screens.title: Loops Compared: For vs For Each vs While
screens.subtitle: When to choose each loop type and common pitfalls

narration.text: Choosing the right loop depends on intent. Use For Loop when you need a fixed count or when the Index is necessary for placement or numbering. Use For Each when working with arrays or collections and when you want concise code that directly accesses elements. Use While when the number of iterations is not known in advance but depends on a condition that changes during runtime. Common mistakes: using While when a simple For would suffice, or forgetting to include a Delay inside a While loop leading to infinite execution. Another frequent error is mutating an array inside a For Each loop which can skip elements or corrupt indexes. Performance considerations: For loops and For Each loops are predictable; avoid repeated expensive calls inside large loops, or move heavy work to timers or deferred tasks. Example contrasts: spawn five cubes — use For; process a player's inventory array — use For Each; continuously check a damage zone every three seconds while the player is alive — use While with Delay. Always prefer clarity and explicit termination conditions to avoid subtle runtime bugs.

keyIdea.title: Pick loops by intent
keyIdea.text: For = fixed count; For Each = array processing; While = condition-driven repetition. Guard While loops to avoid infinite repetition.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Loop Comparison
For Loop
Best for fixed repeat counts and when you need the Index to position or configure instances.
For Each Loop
Best for iterating arrays directly, readable access to each element and its index.
While Loop
Best for condition-driven repetition. Always include Delay or limits to prevent infinite loops.
Decision Table
  • Spawn N objects by index → For Loop.
  • Process each inventory item → For Each Loop.
  • Run repeated checks every few seconds while condition true → While Loop with Delay.
Key Takeaway

Match loop type to intent. Use Delay and limits to keep While loops safe and predictable in the game loop.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Control flow vocabulary to carry forward

narration.text: Remember these concise concepts as you build Blueprints. Control Flow is the order and conditions that determine which nodes run and when. The Branch node implements if-else logic using a Boolean, which is essential for decisions. For Loop iterates a known range and exposes an Index for placement or counting. For Each Loop processes each element of an array, convenient for collections. While Loop repeats while a condition is true but must be guarded with Delay or limits to avoid infinite execution. Sequence fires multiple independent execution paths from a single trigger, useful to organize side effects. Keep these definitions in mind while you practice: they are the building blocks of dynamic and safe gameplay logic. Ask yourself when to use each node and test small examples to internalize their behavior.

keyIdea.title: Core vocabulary
keyIdea.text: Short, precise definitions help you choose the right control-flow node and avoid common mistakes like infinite loops.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Concepts
Branch Node
Executes one of two paths based on a Boolean condition.
For Loop
Iterates a fixed range using a First and Last Index; exposes Index each iteration.
For Each Loop
Processes each element in an array and provides the element and index.
While Loop
Repeats while a condition is true; requires Delay or limits to avoid infinite loops.
Sequence
Fires multiple independent execution paths in order from one event trigger.
Delay
Pauses execution for a duration; useful inside While loops to yield engine time and avoid blocking.
Summary
Match node to intent: Branch for decisions, For/For Each for repetition, While with Delay for conditional checks over time, Sequence to organize multiple starts. Test often and guard loops.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to use while building

narration.text: Keep three compact rules at hand while authoring Blueprints. First, always ensure loop termination: Delay or iteration limits prevent the game from freezing. Second, separate data collection from side effects: gather values in loops and apply UI or state changes after Completed or via Sequence. Third, name Booleans and arrays clearly and use Print String in early tests to observe execution flow. These reminders reduce common wiring errors and make your graphs easier to maintain. As you practice, ask: does this loop need to run every frame? Can I express this check with a Branch plus a timer instead? Small design choices like these prevent subtle runtime issues and make your Blueprints robust. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Guard loops, separate collection from effects, and test with logs. These small practices keep Blueprints safe and debuggable.

Guard loops
Always add Delay or limits to While loops to ensure exit and frame responsiveness.
Separate concerns
Collect data in loops; apply UI and side effects after Completed or via Sequence for consistent state.

Small, safe patterns scale better than clever shortcuts. Use clear conditionals, guarded loops, and orderly sequences to build reliable game mechanics.
